findings.quote: After eleven years of sitting in morning traffic behind a school bus,
findings.note: Sixteen words precede the main subject "I".
"realization" names the act of realizing, and it is carried by the empty verb "come to"; the verb "realize" is available.

findings.quote: The decision to sell was made
findings.note: "decision" is an action noun carried by the empty verb "was made".
"evaluation" is an action noun carried by the empty verb "carried out".
"picturesque" repeats within two sentences; the first occurrence is in the preceding sentence.

findings.quote: I reached the bottom of the hill by seven.
findings.note: Three consecutive sentences follow the same "I left / I reached / I arrived" template; the first is "I left the house at six-forty."

findings.quote: By February I had come to the realization that the side streets were the problem, and I followed the bus routes instead.
findings.note: "bus routes" repeats within three sentences; the first occurrence is "bus routes are cleared first, by six in the morning."
The opening names the car, a new element after a sentence about walking and the neighbourhood. The reader can place it, but the sentence opens on it.
The previous sentence is about the author having forgotten that the distance could be covered another way. This sentence opens on "The walk", a new element that has not appeared in the paragraph.

The previous sentence is about the mechanic's quote for a transmission; the link to the renewal comes only in the trailing phrase 'the same week'. The sentence opens on an element the paragraph has not prepared.

findings.quote: A monthly bus pass costs sixty
findings.note: The previous sentence is about the annual costs of insurance, parking, fuel and repairs; this sentence opens on a bus pass, which nothing earlier in the paragraph has introduced.

findings.quote: My bike was stolen in June.
findings.note: The paragraph was about crossing the Fenwick Road bridge on foot; the bike appears with no earlier mention. The reader cannot connect the theft to the previous sentence.

findings.quote: The combination was forgotten twice in the first week.
findings.note: The opening refers to a combination that is only implied by the lock at the end of the previous sentence. The link sits at the prior sentence's final words.

findings.quote: I left the house at six-forty.
findings.note: The previous sentence was about the route up Carver Hill and its grade; this sentence opens on the speaker's departure time, an element the hill-climb sentence does not prepare.

findings.quote: Municipal snow contracts in our city specify
findings.note: The previous sentence was about arriving at the desk with wet socks and a temper; this sentence opens on municipal snow contracts, an element that arrives without preparation.

findings.quote: The sidewalks along Fenwick Road are cleared
findings.note: The previous sentence ends by naming the bus routes the speaker followed; this sentence opens on the sidewalks of Fenwick Road, a different location than the one just named.

findings.quote: a warm cocoon, an anchor that kept me moored
findings.note: Mixed figure: a cocoon and an anchor moored to concerns cannot both hold as one image. The draft leaves unsettled which claim about the car it is making.

findings.quote: the city opened up like a book
findings.note: Stock image that adds no picture or mechanism beyond the literal claim. The comparison is asserted rather than shown.

findings.quote: It should be noted that I am not trying to tell anyone else how to live. Everyone's situation is different, and what works for one person will not necessarily work for another.
findings.note: Stacked qualification: the disclaimer is stated in one sentence and then restated twice more in the next, with no fact added.

findings.quote: Many people live too far from work, or have children to drop off, or have jobs that require a car, and I do not want to suggest that any of them are doing anything wrong. I can only describe what happened to me, in my own circumstances, which may or may not resemble yours.
findings.note: Stacked qualification: exempts others more than once and adds that circumstances may differ, repeating the earlier hedge.

findings.quote: I pass a picturesque row of Victorian houses on Linden Street, then the picturesque old mill that someone has turned into flats.
findings.note: Repeated example: two sights listed in the same structure, both labelled pleasant-looking, with no separate point.

This paragraph refers to a hill and to a February before the draft has supplied either, and it also presupposes an earlier period when the walk felt like a punishment. The first winter, the climb up Carver Hill and the February realisation are only introduced in the paragraph beginning "The first winter was very hard."
The draft never says who raised the concerns.
The draft never says who should note this. The reader cannot tell who is making this observation or why it is offered.

findings.quote: It was decided in 2023 that all changes would go through this process
findings.note: The draft never says who decided that all changes would go through the board process. That actor is responsible for the decision the paragraph is about, and it cannot be recovered from the surrounding sentences.
The noun "review" carries the action while the verb "conduct" is empty.
"Determination" is buried under the empty verb "makes"; the action is the board's deciding.
Doubled pair: "full" and "complete" say the same thing. The doubled pair occurs in the third sentence.

findings.quote: a toll booth on the highway to production
findings.note: A stock image that restates the delay complaint without adding a mechanism the plain claim would not; the draft never works out what the toll booth corresponds to beyond being an obstacle.

The opening "It" has no referent in the paragraph; the previous sentences were about the board's Thursday meetings and the resulting six-day wait. The decision year is new information placed at the front.
"The handoff" is a new element at the opening; the previous sentence was about raised concerns over delays.

The opening introduces automated logging of approvals as a new element; the previous sentence was about the two-month period giving limited evidence. The link to the preceding material arrives only through the shared term 'lead approvals' later in the sentence.
Restatement: the sentence repeats the point already made in the pilot results about the median wait and the absence of rollbacks.

findings.quote: It should be noted that the board reviewed eleven changes in those two months, compared with more than three hundred in the same period last year.
findings.note: Restatement: the sentence repeats the earlier point that the board reviewed only changes on the high-risk list.
'the pilot' and 'both teams' have no antecedent until the paragraph beginning 'In March and April, the Payments and Search teams ran a pilot.'
The noun decision buries the verb decide behind the empty verb made.
The noun "undertaking" buries the act of undertaking, carried by the empty verb "given".
The noun "assessment" buries the act of assessing, carried by the empty verb "carry out".

findings.quote: At a quarter past four on the ninth of March,
findings.note: Fourteen words precede the main subject "Ellen Morrow".
Four consecutive sentences open with the same words: "She" plus a verb in the past tense (rang, carried, went, left).

findings.quote: In the weeks after the water went down and the loss adjuster had come round to photograph each and every room,
findings.note: The subject "Ellen" arrives after 23 words of introductory clause.

findings.quote: Flood warnings for Quay Street were not issued
findings.note: No issuing body is named here or in the surrounding sentences, and the failure to warn in time is the cost the paragraph is about.
The draft never says who made the promise, though the unkept promise is the claim of responsibility in this sentence.
The opening element, sandbags, has not appeared earlier; the previous sentence concerns flood warnings and the water in the shops.
The previous sentence is about Tom driving to Ashby for flour. The opening is about gluten development, a subject nothing earlier in the paragraph has prepared.

The sentence opens on the street and the flood, neither of which appears in the previous sentence about Ellen's Christmas orders. The reader can place them from earlier in the draft, but the opening is new here.
Opens on Tom, who has not appeared in this paragraph. The previous sentence was about tiles, plaster and the smell of flour.

findings.quote: lit a fire under the council
findings.note: Stock image stacked on the heart-and-body figure in the preceding sentence, so fire and body do not both hold. The draft never says what the support actually did to the council.
Stock image used in place of saying who gave what. The draft supplies no mechanism for how the support arrived or what it changed.
Stock image standing in for an argument the draft never makes about what the street or the council was supposed to learn. It functions as a conclusion the paragraph asserts rather than shows.
"sodden" repeats within two sentences, first appearing in "the smell of sodden flour stayed in the building for weeks."
"whole" repeats within two sentences; the first occurrence is in "a shock to the whole street."
Doubled pair: "each and every" states the same thing twice.
"affected" appears twice within three sentences, first in the paragraph's opening sentence.

findings.quote: Some lost stock and some lost income, and some lost things
findings.note: Three consecutive clauses built on the template "some lost X," adding no structural variation.

findings.quote: The flood affected many people on Quay Street in many different ways. Some lost stock and some lost income, and some lost things that are harder to put a price on. It is difficult to overstate how much the flood affected the people of the street, and it would be impossible to describe every way in which their lives were changed by it.
findings.note: Restatement. The three sentences all assert that the flood affected the street's people in many ways, without adding any new case.

findings.quote: The flood affected many people on Quay Street in many different ways.
findings.note: Repeats the collective-impact claim already made in the paragraph beginning "It was obviously a shock to the whole street.", which had already asserted that the flood struck the whole street; this paragraph restates that general claim in vaguer terms and adds no new particular.
The phrase "arrived at" repeats in the second sentence, where the first occurrence is in the preceding sentence.

findings.quote: It is a feeling that is familiar. It is a feeling that recurs.
findings.note: "It is a feeling that" repeats as a clause opening in two consecutive sentences; the first occurrence is earlier in this paragraph.
"feeling" appears three times within three sentences; the first occurrence is earlier in this paragraph.
"Expectation" is an action noun carried by "was," with "expect" as its verb root.
"Observation" is buried in the empty verb "made"; the action is "observe."
The noun "decision" buries the action, and the empty verb "made" carries it. The committee's deciding is expressed as a noun.
"Conducted" is carried by "was", burying the action in a passive construction.
The draft never says who would make the decision. The actor is left unnamed even though the passive verb is embedded in a clause about the committee's action.
No actor is named for who conducted the meeting.

findings.quote: It was decided by the committee that a decision would be made regarding the proposal.
findings.note: Repeats the paragraph beginning 'It was decided by the committee thxt x determination', restating the same point with no addition.

findings.quote: There was an expectation that a resolution would be arrived at.
findings.note: Repeats the paragraph beginning 'There was an expectation that', restating the same point with no addition.

findings.quote: Some of us left the room with the feeling that nothing had been accomplished.
findings.note: Repeats the paragraph beginning 'Some of us left the room with the feeling', restating the same point with no addition.
